newsitem.title: SPAIN: Fierce competition ex-Madrid to U.S on cargo rates.
newsitem.headline: Fierce competition ex-Madrid to U.S on cargo rates.

text.p: Air cargo rates ex-Madrid are steady -- the downward pressure on North Atlantic prices appears to have abated and tariffs could actually rise on some routes in the coming peak months, airlines and freight forwarders said.
There is still fierce competition on North American routes from Madrid but fewer forwarders and general sales agents reported seeing the cut price offers available in August.
Even so, prices from Madrid to New York's Kennedy airport range from 110 or 120 pesetas a kilo for 100 kilos plus.

Demand was beginning to pick up by mid-September after the slack August period, sales agents said, but the outlook for the peak months of October, November and December is for prices to remain steady in general and perhaps rise on some routes.
The Latin American market is firm, demand for space to the Far East is strong but there is hot competition on the North Atlantic, particularly to New York.

"North Atlantic prices are very low and we've slackened off on North American routes except for specific cargoes. If you lose money on one kilo, then obviously we don't want to fly lots of kilos," said an official at one major European airline.
"We hope North Atlantic prices will rise, but a lot depends on vegetable exports from Spain to the U.S. and Canada in the peak season and how the producers' campaign goes," added a GSA.
Away from the North Atlantic demand and supply are relatively well balanced.
"Prices are stable," said Antoine Esteso, cargo manager at Air France. "I don't think ours will rise from now to the end of the year unless the (franc-peseta) exchange rate moves against us."
Another airline reported good demand from Southern Hemisphere exporters. South Africa for example moves substantial quantities of fish through Spain.
Flights to the Far East are also filling well.
"Demand for space to the Far East, particularly Seoul, Tokyo and Osaka, is rising but prices haven't changed," a GSA said.
A freight forwarder said he had seen higher prices.
"There are space problems to Tokyo and prices are rising," he said.

One of the major European carriers said its ex-Spain business was patchy. There was good demand in Barcelona and from exporters further down the Mediterranean coast but orders were more erratic and prices very competitive on some routes from Madrid.

Some foreign airlines operating from Madrid have already had to resist pressure from their parent companies to raise tariffs on the North Atlantic because they say the market will not allow it. Some fear they may not be able to hold out much longer.

"Our prices haven't changed since November last year. we're not going to raise them now unless headquarters forces us to, but I don't rule out an increase in January," said a GSA with predominantly transatlantic business. --Air Cargo Newsroom Tel+44 171 542 7706 Fax +44 171 542 5017
